The Story of Shivbhooti the Priest

I bow to Lord Jina, who brings welfare to the world, and I write this story about the evils of bad company, so that people may strive to avoid the company of wicked ones.

This story is set in the time when King Dhanpal ruled Kaushambi. Dhanpal was wise and cared for his subjects. His enemies trembled at his name. The king had a royal priest named Shivbhooti, who was well-versed in the Puranas.

In that same city lived two Shudras named Kalppal and Poornachandra. They possessed some wealth. Poornachandra's wife was named Maniprabha, and they had a daughter named Sumitra. When Sumitra's wedding came, Poornachandra invited his caste-brothers and, being somewhat acquainted with the royal priest, invited him as well. But the priest raised an objection: "Brother, I cannot eat your food." Then Kalppal interceded, saying, "Very well! You need not eat our food directly. We shall have Brahmins prepare the meal for you, so you will have no objection." The priest, after all, was a Brahmin, and the famous saying applies: "Discontented Brahmins are ruined" — meaning Brahmins fall to ruin through greed. Unable to resist the temptation of a free meal, he agreed, reasoning that since Brahmins would cook it, there could be no harm. He did not consider that even if Brahmins cooked, the money was the Shudra's — who knows through what sins it was earned.

At the appointed time, the food was prepared. On one side sat the priest, on the other Poornachandra's family — each with separate dining enclosures. The priest ate heartily, as though he had never enjoyed such a feast before. Some people saw him dining there and reported it to the king. The king, deeming it unfit to keep in his kingdom a Brahmin who dined with Shudras and trampled upon caste order, banished him from the land. Truly it is said: "Bad company surely brings suffering."

The lesson is clear: even a learned man falls when he keeps bad company and yields to greed for a single meal. The priest's learning and position could not save him once he compromised his principles for worldly gain.
